title: Interacting with educational chatbots: A systematic review
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the growing use of chatbots in education and the lack of a focused synthesis of how educational chatbots are designed, interacted with, and evaluated. The authors specifically aim to analyze evidence-based chatbot-learner interaction design techniques, as well as the field of application, platform, educational role, interaction style, design principles, empirical evidence, and limitations across prior studies.

The study is a systematic review of 36 articles published between 2011 and 2021, identified through searches in ACM Digital Library, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and SpringerLink. The reviewed chatbots span multiple educational contexts, including computer science, general education, language learning, mathematics, and other smaller application areas. Most systems were web-based and commonly served as teaching agents or peer agents; interaction styles were usually chatbot-driven and often flow-based or intent-based, with fewer user-driven systems.

The review finds that educational chatbots are frequently designed around personalized learning, experiential learning, social dialogue, collaborative learning, affective learning, learning by teaching, and scaffolding. Empirical evidence in the reviewed studies generally suggests improved learning, engagement, satisfaction, or interest, though the authors note uneven methodological quality and a lack of attention to usability heuristics. Overall, the paper concludes that educational chatbots show promise, but future work should better address design quality, localization, personality, and more robust evaluation.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Conversational/educational chatbot or conversational agent used in educational settings to tutor, answer questions, provide feedback, scaffold interaction, or support learning tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a systematic review of 36 educational chatbot studies, examining their fields of application, platforms, roles, interaction styles, design principles, evaluation methods, and limitations.

findings.finding_summary: Across 36 reviewed papers, the authors report that educational chatbots were mainly used as teaching agents or peer agents, most often on web platforms. The review synthesis indicates that more than a third of the chatbots were evaluated with experiments and that results primarily point to improved learning and subjective satisfaction.
findings.measure: Review synthesis of reported evaluation outcomes across included chatbot studies

findings.finding_summary: The review found that most chatbot studies used chatbot-driven, flow-based interaction styles, while a smaller set used user-driven conversations. The paper reports that some systems included personalized learning, experiential learning, collaborative learning, affective learning, learning by teaching, and scaffolding, with the overall evidence base suggesting improved learning, engagement, and satisfaction in several studies.
findings.measure: Review synthesis of interaction styles, design principles, and reported outcomes

quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review of prior chatbot studies rather than a new controlled trial. The evidence is synthesized from heterogeneous studies, with the paper itself not reporting a single pooled effect size.
impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests generally positive educational effects, but the paper does not provide a quantitative aggregate effect size for teacher coaching or reflective-practice uptake. Reported impacts are qualitative and broad rather than precise.
